description: Inversis is a NASA-powered crop-rotation decision-support project. We're building a transparent system that uses NASA Earth observations and agronomic constraints to compare rotation strategies across historical conditions. Rather than simply recommending a rotation, Inversis tests how decisions change under different assumptions, identifies evidence that could overturn them, and makes uncertainty visible. We prioritize scientific rigor, reproducibility, and transparent decision-making.
summary:
A crop-rotation decision should answer more than which plan ranks first. Inversis asks what could change the decision and when the evidence is insufficient to make one.

Built for Field Shift, Inversis uses ten years of NASA POWER daily maximum temperatures and GPM IMERG precipitation (2015–2024) for a gridded study location in Romania’s Bărăgan Plain. It compares three five-year crop sequences across six overlapping historical replays using minimax regret. Alternative A has the lowest modeled exposure in 2015–2019 and Alternative B in 2018–2022, yet Baseline limits the worst relative disadvantage across all six.

Users can challenge the comparison by changing preferences, provisional crop windows, and hypothetical crop permissions. When no candidate remains eligible, Inversis refuses to invent a selection. A separate Field Evidence & Readiness workflow captures unverified local soil and crop-history information, while downloadable SHA-256 records trace the decision to source evidence and calculations.

Inversis is a working, reproducible historical-exposure decision prototype, not a yield forecast or validated agronomic recommendation.
details:
The problem and our approach

Choosing a crop rotation under changing environmental conditions involves more than identifying the lowest numerical score. Different plans encounter different historical exposures, farmer constraints can invalidate seemingly preferable options, and missing field information can make a precise-looking recommendation misleading.

Inversis is a working decision-assurance prototype that makes those dependencies visible. Rather than treating NASA Earth observations as an automatic crop recommendation, it connects historical evidence to a conditional comparison, tests the assumptions behind that comparison, and preserves a reproducible record of what the evidence establishes.

How Inversis works

The prototype studies a gridded location in Romania's Bărăgan Plain, explicitly distinguished from a measured farm. It uses NASA POWER daily maximum 2-metre air temperature and NASA GPM IMERG Final V07B daily precipitation for 2015–2024: 3,653 validated daily values from each source.

Three ordered five-year crop sequences are evaluated across six overlapping five-year historical replays. Within provisional crop-specific calendar windows, Inversis calculates two environmental indicators: the fraction of days reaching at least 35°C and the longest consecutive period with precipitation below 1 mm/day.

These physical exposures are normalized against declared reference ranges and combined using adjustable illustrative preference weights. A minimax-regret calculation identifies the candidate whose largest disadvantage relative to the best eligible candidate in any shared replay is smallest. The application exposes the underlying losses, comparisons, assumptions, and calculations rather than presenting an unexplained ranking.

What the results reveal

At equal heat and dry-spell weights, Baseline has the lowest maximum regret (0.0481), compared with 0.1364 for Alternative A and 0.1712 for Alternative B.

But Baseline is not the lowest-exposure plan in every historical replay. Alternative A leads in 2015–2019, while Alternative B leads in 2018–2022. This demonstrates why the overall minimax decision and the best result in an individual historical period are different questions.

Users can explore 21 tested preference combinations, five crop-window shifts, alternative normalization, and historical sensitivity diagnostics. Baseline remains selected throughout these declared tests, although the numerical margins change. This is bounded model stability, not proof of universal resilience.

The interactive Next Evidence workflow also explores hypothetical farmer permissions. Prohibiting soybean leaves Baseline as the sole eligible candidate, without establishing competitive superiority. Prohibiting sunflower leaves no eligible rotation, and Inversis explicitly refuses to manufacture a replacement recommendation.

Connecting environmental evidence to the field

The Field Evidence & Readiness workbench allows users to record local soil pH, texture, organic matter, drainage, irrigation, preceding crops, disease history, and crop timing, each with an explicit source classification.

All information begins as unknown. User-supplied values are distinguished from independently validated environmental-source processing and are not silently converted into agronomic rules. The interface identifies additional field assessments needed before interpreting the modeled comparison as an agricultural decision.

This directly supports the challenge's emphasis on soil information, crop characteristics, and farmer priorities while preserving the difference between recording evidence and validating its agricultural meaning.

Reproducibility and technical implementation

Inversis preserves original NASA source records, retrieval information, processing lineage, and file hashes. Its downloadable canonical JSON decision certificate includes assumptions, scenario comparisons, diagnostic results, limitations, and a verifiable SHA-256 fingerprint.

The implementation uses TypeScript, React, and Vite, with Python and HDF5-based scientific verification tools. It is deployed publicly through GitHub Pages, requires no login, and contains no runtime generative AI.

The completed application passed 142 automated tests, four separate computational scientific checks, and validation of all 3,653 original IMERG daily files. These checks establish reproducibility and tested computational correctness, not independent agronomic certification. OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT assisted implementation, verification, documentation, and presentation development; the numerical decisions are deterministic calculations from retrieved NASA evidence, not AI-generated conclusions.

Innovation, intended impact, and next steps

Inversis's innovation is not a newly invented optimization algorithm. It is the integration of real Earth-observation evidence, transparent comparison, assumption testing, eligibility-aware refusal, local information review, and reproducible decision records into one usable workflow.

The intended users are farmers, agricultural advisers, and researchers who need to understand why a provisional decision is preferred, what could change it, and which evidence is still missing.

Inversis does not currently predict yields, quantify soil-health improvement, establish biological rotation benefits, or certify field suitability. Its thresholds and crop windows are illustrative, and the six historical replays are overlapping rather than independent samples.

The next scientific stage would integrate authenticated local soil assessments, locally validated crop-specific response functions, agronomic suitability constraints, and feedback from agricultural professionals.

The goal is to make agricultural decisions more transparent and evidence-qualified—not merely more automated.
